Chapter 3 of 6

The incident

What you will see

About 20 minutes. A new release of the stock lookup service makes every stock request slow. The team ships it as a canary with 10% of the traffic. You run the canary check, it fails, and you roll back before the other 90% of lookups are affected. Then you use Datadog on the canary's traffic to show that the cause is in the release code, not in the stream.

Needs: one more layer, releases. Lab 3.1 starts by turning it on (skip that if you chose everything at once).

Lab 3.1: The incident #

A release is one deployed build of the lookup service, identified by its version. 1.0.0 is healthy. 1.1.0 adds product details by preparing a product catalogue inside every request: the regression. 1.2.0 prepares the catalogue once at startup: the fix. The load balancer (ALB) rule for /api/availability/* sends requests to the three releases by weight, one target group per release.

The ALB moves the traffic and Datadog compares the versions. The gate (canary-check, or Check canary in the panel) says pass or stop, but only when you run it: nothing runs it for you.

Why the comparison between versions is fair

All three releases run on the same Fargate task size (0.5 vCPU / 1 GB, service_sizing in terraform/aws/variables.tf). Any difference in latency or CPU between versions therefore comes from the code, not from the task size.

Open this Chapter in the demo home, group "3. The incident": lookup p95 by version, ECS CPU against the task's whole vCPU and unhealthy targets, with the Amazon ECS events as markers, and links to APM and the 1.1.0 traces.

Turn on the releases layer #

Skip this if you chose everything at once, or if releases is already in your layers: line (make layers-status shows releases: ON).

  1. In demo.yaml, change the line to layers: core,releases (keep any other layers you already added).

  2. Run:

    Terminal (both paths)
    make layer-on L=releases CONFIRM=yes

    Wait until the ECS services are healthy before you continue; give it a few minutes.

    What this creates

    This creates the p95-by-version monitor in Datadog and starts the two Fargate services for releases 1.1.0 and 1.2.0 (0.5 vCPU and 1 GB each, about $0.02 per hour each at the prices in Reference D).

  3. Check the layer: make layers-status should print releases: ON.

1. Check that routing works from your machine #

With the control panel

In the control panel, open the Release routing card and press Refresh weights. The tiles should read 100% for 1.0.0 and 0% for 1.1.0 and 1.2.0.

Why the panel needs no AWS login

The panel changes the routing from AWS itself, so it does not need your AWS login.

With the terminal

The routing commands call the AWS API, so they need a valid aws login session.

Terminal (both paths)
make route-check
Expected output
alb-routing: live weights 1.0.0/1.1.0/1.2.0 = 100 0 0%

If it fails, run aws login --profile dd-demo and try again.

2. Ship 1.1.0 as a 10% canary #

With the control panel

  1. In the control panel, press Full demo reset on the Demo reset card and confirm. It stops background sales and sets the routing to 100 / 0 / 0. Wait for full-reset succeeded.
  2. Press Canary 1.1.0 (10%) on the Release routing card and confirm. The tiles should read 90% for 1.0.0, 10% for 1.1.0 and 0% for 1.2.0, and the line under them Live 90/10/0 · previous (for Rollback): 100/0/0.

With the terminal

Terminal (both paths)
make reset
make canary-110-10
make route-show

canary-110-10 first prints the AWS rule JSON. The last lines should be:

Expected output
...
alb-routing: weights 1.0.0/1.1.0/1.2.0 = 90 10 0%
alb-routing: live weights 1.0.0/1.1.0/1.2.0 = 90 10 0%
current=90 10 0 previous=100 0 0

3. Generate steady load #

You send 5 requests per second for 2 minutes.

With the control panel

In the control panel, press Run load (120 s, 5 rps) on the Checks card and confirm.

With the terminal

Terminal (both paths)
make load LOAD_DURATION=120 LOAD_RPS=5

You should see one JSON line per 10 s window with both releases, then a summary. The gate reads this summary.

More about this step

Why load. The gate and Datadog both need enough requests on the canary to measure it.

With the control panel

What the card shows while it runs. During the 2 minutes the card shows live progress lines, for example Load 40/120 s, last window: ..., then the requests, errors, p50 and p95 per release. The buttons stay disabled until the run ends. The gate reads the summary of this run.

With the terminal

What the load prints.

Expected output
{"window": 0, "window_s": 10, "count": 50, "releases": {"1.0.0": {"count": <n>, "errors": 0, ...}, "1.1.0": {"count": <n>, "errors": 0, ...}}}
...
{"summary": {"total": {"count": 600, "releases": {"1.0.0": {...}, "1.1.0": {...}}}, ...}}

How many samples to expect. About one lookup in ten goes to 1.1.0, so expect about 60 samples of it in two minutes.

While it runs: watch the shop footer. While the load runs, keep the product page open and watch the footer: about once every ten seconds it shows "Serving release 1.1.0" for a second. The split is per request, not per user, and the page asks for the stock every second, so about one answer in ten comes from the slow release. That is too little to notice in the shop, which is why the canary gate and p95 by version in APM (step 6) are what catch it.

4. Run the gate: it fails #

The gate compares the canary (1.1.0) with the release it would replace (1.0.0).

With the control panel

  1. In the control panel, press Verify on the Checks card and wait for VERIFY PASSED with 0 position and 0 sellable mismatches.
  2. Press Check canary and confirm.

You should see: Verify passes, because the stock numbers are right (1.1.0 is slow, not wrong). Then Check canary fails on latency only: the result box shows CANARY GATES FAILED: p95 1.1.0 <ms> ms > budget 200 ms; roll back, with several hundred ms against the 200 ms budget. Only the p95_b line is FAIL; the sample, error-rate and correctness gates are PASS.

With the terminal

Terminal (both paths)
make verify
make canary-check CHECK_ARGS="--release-a 1.0.0 --release-b 1.1.0 --min-samples 30 --verify-file /out/verify.json"

You should see: make verify passes with 0 mismatches, because the stock numbers are right (1.1.0 is slow, not wrong). Then the gate fails on latency only, with a p95 of several hundred ms against the 200 ms budget:

Expected output
PASS min_samples_a: release 1.0.0: <n> samples, need >= 30
PASS min_samples_b: release 1.1.0: <n> samples, need >= 30
PASS error_rate_a: release 1.0.0: 0/<n> errors (0.0000), max 0.0
PASS error_rate_b: release 1.1.0: 0/<n> errors (0.0000), max 0.0
FAIL p95_b: release 1.1.0: p95 <ms> ms, budget 200 ms
PASS correctness: verify: 0 mismatch(es)
CANARY GATES FAILED: p95 1.1.0 <ms> ms > budget 200 ms; roll back

That is the expected result: the answers are correct and there are no errors, but the canary is too slow, so the rollout stops here.

More about this step

What the gate checks. It requires at least 30 samples of each, no errors, a canary p95 of 200 ms or less, and a passing verify. The default minimum is 100 samples, but a 10% share gives only about 60 in two minutes, so at 10% the gate lowers it to 30.

With the control panel

Which gate the card picks. With the routing at 90 / 10 / 0, the card picks this gate by itself and shows it below the buttons as CHECK_ARGS="--release-a 1.0.0 --release-b 1.1.0 --min-samples 30 --verify-file /out/verify.json".

With the control panel

The status line. The status line reads canary-check failed: CANARY GATES FAILED: p95 1.1.0 <ms> ms > budget 200 ms; roll back ....

With the terminal

Exit code, and running it without CHECK_ARGS. The command exits with a non-zero code. Without CHECK_ARGS, make canary-check reads the live routing and picks the same gate; the explicit form above shows what it checks.

5. Roll back #

With the control panel

In the control panel, press Rollback on the Release routing card and confirm. The tiles should read 100 / 0 / 0 again, the split before the last change, and the line under them Live 100/0/0 · previous (for Rollback): 90/10/0.

With the terminal

Terminal (both paths)
make rollback
make route-show
Expected output
...
current=100 0 0 previous=90 10 0

Only the 10% of lookups that went to 1.1.0 during the canary were slow. The other 90% never reached it.

Where the evidence is

The canary's traces stay in Datadog, so you can now look for the cause while shoppers use the healthy release.

6. Compare releases in APM #

Open the APM inventory-api 1.1.0: link within 15 minutes of the load (later, set the time range to when the load ran) and look at the Deployments section of the service page. You should see 1.1.0 far above 1.0.0 in p95 latency.

Two more views, our numbers, and why the three numbers differ

Without the link: APM > inventory-api with environment dd-demo-hybrid, the load window, operation flask.request, and the filter resource_name:get_/api/availability/_product_id (the APM link redirects to /apm/entity/service:inventory-api). Each Deployments row is one version, with its p95 latency and error rate. After the canary ends, the only 1.1.0 traffic is the load balancer's health checks (get_/readyz, about 6 per minute per version), so a later or longer window without that filter shows a 1.1.0 p95 of about 2 ms. During the canary, 1.1.0 is far above 1.0.0 at p95: around a second or more, against under ten milliseconds.

You can read the comparison in three places. The first is the Deployments section above; the other two follow.

In our run (2026-10-06, every release on 0.5 vCPU) the load script measured a client-side p95 of about 1.5 s for 1.1.0 and about 10 ms for 1.0.0 at 90 / 10 / 0. Your numbers will differ.

  1. To see the same number as a graph, open Metrics > Explorer and paste this query (the environment in angle brackets is yours: dd-demo- followed by your stack name; a connected guide fills it in):

    Expected output
    p95:trace.flask.request{env:<env>,service:inventory-api,resource_name:get_/api/availability/_product_id} by {version}

    Set the time range to the load window. You should see one line per version.

  2. To see the load balancer's measurement, open Metrics > Explorer with the AWS integration's metric (the name in angle brackets is dd-demo- followed by your stack name; a connected guide fills it in):

    Expected output
    avg:aws.applicationelb.target_response_time.p95{name:<stack name>} by {targetgroup}

    The AWS integration publishes the percentile as a separate metric (.p95), so take its average by target group. You should see the target group of 1.1.0 (inventory-110) well above the others. The AWS integration sends this metric once per minute.

Why the three numbers differ. The load script's p95, the one the gate checks, is measured end to end through the load balancer. It includes the time a request waits while the slow release is busy. The load balancer's target response time starts when the request is sent to the task and ends when the first byte comes back. The APM span measures only the handler inside the service, so it does not see time spent waiting before the handler starts.

The three numbers agree when no requests wait, as on 1.0.0 and 1.2.0. Use the APM number to say how much time the code takes, and the client number to say what a shopper experienced.

7. Open one slow trace #

From the APM service page, open Traces filtered to version:1.1.0 and open a slow request's trace. You should see a catalogue.prepare span that takes most of the request time and a short stock.read span (the Redis reads).

More about this step

If you do not see the spans. If the trace does not show them at first, switch to the Waterfall view and look for catalogue.prepare and stock.read there.

Optional, with the dd-rum layer: start from the shopper's side. Optional, with the dd-rum layer on: the Online shop's RUM SDK adds trace headers to its own /api/ calls, so you can also start from the shopper's side. In RUM, open a session of your product page from the canary window, choose a slow /api/availability/... resource and open its trace. It opens the same inventory-api trace with catalogue.prepare.

What just happened: every span carries the unified service tags env, service and version, so APM can compare releases directly, even when one of them got only a tenth of the traffic. The catalogue work uses CPU and runs again in every request, so latency grows with load, while the Redis read stays fast.

8. Rule out the stream #

On the stock dashboard the Freshness group has not changed, and the Service objective group shows inventory-api lookup p95 by version (s) rising for 1.1.0 only.

The DSM map and the p95 monitor

The DSM map shows the same healthy edges as in Lab 1.1. The monitor "[dd-demo-hybrid] inventory-api p95 latency above 0.2s on 1.1.0" can go to Alert after its evaluation window, depending on how many 1.1.0 samples fell into that window.

9. Optional: see what skipping the gate would have done #

To see the effect without a canary, send all traffic to 1.1.0 once, send load for about 2 minutes, then switch back to the healthy release.

Try it: all traffic to 1.1.0, and what happened in our run

With the control panel

  1. In the control panel, press Incident (all to 1.1.0) on the Release routing card and confirm. The tiles read 0 / 100 / 0.
  2. Press Run load (120 s, 5 rps) on the Checks card and wait for the run to end.
  3. Press Baseline (all to 1.0.0). The tiles read 100 / 0 / 0.

With the terminal

Terminal (both paths)
make incident

Then send load. It runs for about 2 minutes:

Terminal (both paths)
make load LOAD_DURATION=120 LOAD_RPS=5

When it ends, switch back to the healthy release:

Terminal (both paths)
make route-baseline

While the load runs, every lookup goes to 1.1.0 and requests queue up. On 0.5 vCPU, 1.1.0 cannot keep up with 5 requests per second. In our run (2026-10-06) 532 of the 600 requests timed out on the client, the 15 that were answered had a p95 of about 9.4 s, the task used its whole 0.5 vCPU, and ECS replaced it after it failed its health check. This is what the 10% canary kept away from 90% of the lookups. To see it in Datadog, open the demo home, group "3. The incident", and use its link "The night of the incident": it opens the same dashboard on 2026-10-06 18:10-18:30 UTC, our run, where ECS CPU of 1.1.0 stays at 100% for about four minutes, the target turns unhealthy and the Amazon ECS events show the task being replaced. That fixed window has data only on the stack hybrid; for your own run, set the time picker to the minutes of your load. ECS starts a new 1.1.0 task by itself; Lab 4.1 does not need it. This run also gives you the CPU comparison under the same load that you use at the end of Lab 4.1.

Checkpoint #

  • The gate reported CANARY GATES FAILED with a FAIL line for p95_b on release 1.1.0 (step 4).
  • After the rollback, the routing is back to 100 / 0 / 0. Control panel: the Release routing tiles read 100 / 0 / 0 · Terminal: make route-show reads 100 0 0 (step 5).
  • APM shows a much higher p95 for 1.1.0 than for 1.0.0, and a 1.1.0 trace shows catalogue.prepare (steps 6 and 7).
  • The Freshness group shows no change (step 8).

Summary

The failed gate stopped the slow release at 10%, and the rollback removed it. The version tags changed "the canary is slow" into "release 1.1.0 prepares a catalogue in every request". Do not reset: Lab 4.1 starts from 100 / 0 / 0.

Switch to the terminal path?

Pick one path and use it from start to finish. The control panel and the terminal each remember their own last routing for Rollback, so mixing them in one run can roll back to the wrong state. Switch only if you are starting a lab from a reset.
